6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 9
Dor Minzer
So far we studied the models of DFAs, NFAs, PDAs and CFGs, and their power. By that, we mean the
classes of languages that they can recognize, i.e., regular languages and context free languages. While these
classes are important and they have some applications by themselves, the primary goal of this discussion was
to set up the correct mindset with respect to how to formalize computation. Today, we will define a much
more important and central computational model, known as Turing Machines (TMs in short). While on the
surface level TMs will look like a small variation on our models thus far, they are a completely different
beast, and in principle they are able to compute anything that a modern computer can.

Design a Turing machine for the language L = {w ∈{0, 1}∗| w = wR}.
Solution:
We start reading the input, look at its first symbol, remember it in our state and then replace
it by ⊥. We then traverse to the end of the input to the last letter, and check if it is equal to the letter we
remember in our state. If it is not, we reject. If it is, we replace it by ⊥, go back to the first non ⊥symbol in
the input, and repeat the process. If we replaced the whole input with ⊥, we accept.

The name “language” hints at the origin of this notion, but I encourage you to think of a language L as a
problem. For example, consider the computation problem whose input is a string x ∈{0, 1}∗, and the goal
is to count the parity of the number of 1’s in it. The language we associate with this problem is
L = {x ∈{0, 1}∗| x has an even number of 1’s}.
The point here is that if we are able to tell whether a given input x is in L or not, then we have solved the
aforementioned computational problem.

2. Σ is the alphabet (i.e., a finite set of symbols).
3. q0 ∈Q is the initial state of M.
4. F ⊆Q is the set of accepting states of M.

d2c95543-f228-475d-b8f3-0b37d1307ee2.name: Random Access Machine (RAM)
d2c95543-f228-475d-b8f3-0b37d1307ee2.definition: A model of computation characterized by having a small number of registers capable of mathematical operations and a large memory accessible via load/store operations, mimicking low-level programming languages.

citations.snippet:
1.3
Random Access Machines (RAM)
We now describe a model of computation which is more in line with low-level programming languages, such
as assembly. In this model, the machine has very few registers R1, . . . , Rk, which it can do mathematical
operations on. Additionally, the machine has memory m1, . . . , mn which is much larger in comparison, but
the machine cannot do any operations on it, other than load from it or save to it. Lastly, the machine has
a certain list of operations it can use: LOAD, ADD, STORE, EQUAL, SUBTRACT, all with the obvious
interpretation. With this in mind, an example RAM program takes the following form:
1. LOAD R1 ←m1.
2. LOAD R2 ←m2.
3. ADD R3 ←R1, R2.
4. LOAD R4 ←m17
5. EQUAL R4, R3.
6. STORE R4 →m33.

1.5
The Church-Turing Thesis
The Church-Turing thesis is somewhat of an informal assertion, stating that anything “computable” can
be computed by the model of Turing machines. What is actually meant by it, is that the model of Turing
machines we defined faithfully captures what we believe we can compute in the world (ignoring notions of
efficiency for the time being), and the results we saw today give some supporting evidence for that: we saw
several ways of strengthening the model, and they all turned out to be equivalent to the standard model. At

Lecture 13
Dor Minzer
In the last lecture we proved that ATM is not decidable via a diagonalization argument. We then defined
the halting problem HTM and showed that it is also not decidable. The proof for that did not go through
a diagonalization again. Instead, we showed that if we had a decider for HTM, then we could use it to
construct a decider for ATM, thus reaching a contradiction. This proof technique is called reduction. We
denote the fact that “a decider for HTM can be used to construct a decider for ATM” by
ATM ⩽HTM.

aligns well with what to intend.

Dor Minzer
In the last lecture we proved that ATM is not decidable via a diagonalization argument. We then defined
the halting problem HTM and showed that it is also not decidable. The proof for that did not go through
a diagonalization again. Instead, we showed that if we had a decider for HTM, then we could use it to
construct a decider for ATM, thus reaching a contradiction. This proof technique is called reduction. We
denote the fact that “a decider for HTM can be used to construct a decider for ATM” by
ATM ⩽HTM.
One way to remember the direction here is to interpret the inequality sign as “not harder than”, and then it
aligns well with what to intend.

that HTM̸ ∈coRE.

6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 13
Dor Minzer
In the last lecture we proved that ATM is not decidable via a diagonalization argument. We then defined
the halting problem HTM and showed that it is also not decidable. The proof for that did not go through
a diagonalization again. Instead, we showed that if we had a decider for HTM, then we could use it to
construct a decider for ATM, thus reaching a contradiction. This proof technique is called reduction. We
denote the fact that “a decider for HTM can be used to construct a decider for ATM” by
ATM ⩽HTM.
One way to remember the direction here is to interpret the inequality sign as “not harder than”, and then it
aligns well with what to intend.

6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 16
Dor Minzer
Last time we defined the notion of time complexity and the class DTIME(t(n)). Today, we will state
and prove the time hierarchy theorem and define the class P.
1
The Time Hierarchy Theorem
Below we state and prove a weak version of the time hierarchy theorem.
Definition 1.1. A function t: N →N is called time-constructible if there is a TM M that on input n runs

6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 13
Dor Minzer
In the last lecture we proved that ATM is not decidable via a diagonalization argument. We then defined
the halting problem HTM and showed that it is also not decidable. The proof for that did not go through
a diagonalization again. Instead, we showed that if we had a decider for HTM, then we could use it to
construct a decider for ATM, thus reaching a contradiction. This proof technique is called reduction. We
denote the fact that “a decider for HTM can be used to construct a decider for ATM” by
ATM ⩽HTM.
One way to remember the direction here is to interpret the inequality sign as “not harder than”, and then it
aligns well with what to intend.

Proof. This can be proved by diagonalization via a suitable adaptation of the proof of Theorem 1.2, and you
are encouraged to work out the details. Here, we give a different proof that builds towards a more general
method.
Assume towards contradiction that HTM ∈R, and let H be a decider for HTM. Consider the TM H′
that on input y works as follows:
1. Check if y is of the form (⟨M⟩, x) for some TM M, and else reject.
2. Run H(⟨M⟩, x):
(a) If it accepts, run M on x and accept/reject accordingly.
(b) If it rejects, reject.
Note that H′ is a valid TM, and also that it always halts. Indeed, the first step always halts, and as H always
halts, the check in the second step also always halts. If H(⟨M⟩, x) accepts, then by choice of H we get that
M(x) halts, so if we run 2(a) that run will halt.

natural and nice problems are NP-complete. Towards this end, we have the following lemma.

NP-hard.

to xi = 1 and taking bi corresponds to xi = 0. Thus, if we take t which has all 1’s in the left block, this will
force the solution S in the SubsetSum problem to pick either ai or bi for each i, so implicitly it will encode
an assignment to φ.
What about the right block? The goal here is to account for which clauses are being satisfied. Indeed, if
xi appears in clauses Cj and Ck and we decide to assign xi = 1, then this choice immediately means that
Cj and Ck are satisfied (regardless of the rest of the assignment). So, a natural choice for the second block
in t is to be all 1’s, but it doesn’t quite work: it may be the case that for a clause Cj, the assignment gives
all of the literals

a construction which cannot be colored with 3 colors if x1, x2, x3 are all green, but that can be 3-colored if
at least one of them is red. We call this gadget H(x1, x2, x3).
With this in mind, if Cj is a clause of φ, say Cj = (xi ∨xj ∨xk), then we add to the graph G a copy of
H(xi, xj, xk), where the input vertices are the vertices labeled by xi, xj and xk from the variable gadgets.

inputs of the gadget are the vertices labeled by xi, xj and xk in the variable gadgets.

7371e1a9-cfb8-4acb-a8e9-888799e472b7.name: 3-Coloring Problem
7371e1a9-cfb8-4acb-a8e9-888799e472b7.definition: A graph coloring problem where vertices of a graph are colored with three colors such that no edge connects two vertices of the same color.

citations.snippet:
2
3-Coloring
Let G = (V, E) be a graph. We say that G is 3-colorable if there exists a map χ: V →{red, blue, green}
such that for each e = {u, v} ∈E we have that χ(u)̸ = χ(v). In other words, if there is a way to color the
vertices of G, in which no edge is monochromatic. We define the language
3Coloring = {⟨G⟩| G is a 3-colorable graph}.
In the recitation you showed that if we replace the 3 above by a 2, then the problem is in P. It turns out that
3Coloring is much harder:
Theorem 2.1. 3Coloring is NP-complete.
Proof. The proof that 3Coloring is in NP is straightforward and is left to the reader, and we next show
NP-hardness. For that, we show that 3SAT ⩽p 3Coloring. Fix a 3CNF formula φ and construct a graph G
as follows. The main point again is to create a mechanism in the context of 3C

6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 7
Dor Minzer
In this lecture, we will describe an automaton-type model of computation that corresponds to context
free languages. Note that, whereas for regular languages we began with such a definition and later proved
equivalence to other models, for context free languages we did not do so. Instead, we started off with a
definition via grammars, which is somewhat close in spirit to regular expressions. We did so because the
automaton model that corresponds to CFLs, called pushdown automata (abbreviated PDA), is much less
natural than DFAs or grammars. However, it is useful when studying CFLs.
PDAs are computational models that are inherently non-deterministic. Informally, a PDA is an NFA that
has an additional way to store memory

Boolean Formulas
Recall that a Boolean formula φ(x1, . . . , xn) is a formula on the variables x1, . . . , xn using the operations
of negation, OR, AND. For example,
φ(x1, . . . , xn) = x1 ∧(x2 ∨x3) ∧( ¯x5 ∨¯x7 ∨¯x1) ∨x17
is a Boolean formula. A CNF formula is a Boolean formula that takes the form
φ(x1, . . . , xn) = C1 ∧C2 ∧. . . ∧Cm,
where each Ci is called a clause, and is an OR of literals. A 3-CNF formula is a CNF formula in which
each clause contains 3 literals. A Boolean formula φ is called satisfiable if there exists an assignment
A: {x1, . . . , xn} →{0, 1} such that φ(A(x1), . . . , A(xn)) = 1. We define the languages SAT, CNF-SAT
and 3SAT correspondingly:

of negation, OR, AND. For example,
φ(x1, . . . , xn) = x1 ∧(x2 ∨x3) ∧( ¯x5 ∨¯x7 ∨¯x1) ∨x17
is a Boolean formula. A CNF formula is a Boolean formula that takes the form
φ(x1, . . . , xn) = C1 ∧C2 ∧. . . ∧Cm,
where each Ci is called a clause, and is an OR of literals. A 3-CNF formula is a CNF formula in which
each clause contains 3 literals. A Boolean formula φ is called satisfiable if there exists an assignment
A: {x1, . . . , xn} →{0, 1} such that φ(A(x1), . . . , A(xn)) = 1. We define the languages SAT, CNF-SAT
and 3SAT correspondingly:

a6a4da00-284f-4575-be8b-8d01ba698432.name: SAT is in NP
a6a4da00-284f-4575-be8b-8d01ba698432.definition: The Boolean satisfiability problem is a member of the complexity class NP since there is a polynomial-time verifier that checks satisfiability of a given assignment.

Proof of Theorem 1.1
A polynomial-time verifier for SAT, V (⟨φ⟩, w), thinks of the witness w as an assignment to the variables of
φ, and check that it is indeed satisfying. It is easy to see that this is indeed a polynomial time verifier, so we
get that SAT ∈NP. The rest of the proof is devoted to showing that SAT is NP-hard.
By definition, we need to show a polynomial time reduction from any language in NP to SAT. Fix
L ∈NP and let N be a NTM for L running in time nc, where c > 0 is some constant. We will describe a
polynomial time reduction
f(x) = ⟨φN,x⟩,
so that if x ∈L then φN,x is satisfiable, and if x̸ ∈L, then φN,x is not satisfiable.

Today we are going to define regular expressions and show that they characterize regular languages.

Regular Expressions

Dor Minzer
Today we are going to define regular expressions and show that they characterize regular languages.

Regular Expressions

also regular. That gives us a recipe to generate a bunch of regular languages from L1, L2.

1.4
Membership in a Context Free Grammar
Suppose you are given a grammar G and an input string x ∈Σ∗. How can you tell if x ∈L(G) or not?
When we discussed regular languages, we could simply run the DFA and check if it accepts or not. However,
here it is not clear how to solve this task. We can start trying to use derivation rules to get to x, but there are
infinitely many ways of applying the rules, and it not clear when we can call it quits and say that we tried all
of the “relevant” chains of applications.
Intuitively, it makes sense that if x has length n, then the chain of derivation for x in G shouldn’t be
much longer than O(n). However, strictly speaking this may not be the case, as there could be derivations
that derive the empty string.

1. Q is a finite set of states.
2. Σ is the alphabet of the input.

Note that in our prior PDA constructions, we used the feature of
checking if the stack is empty. This feature, however, is non-existent in the formal definition, which means

citations.snippet:
The key feature here is that the left transition pushes t to the stack, and the right transition pops t from
the stack. Thus, if we make the first transition, then go from r to s in some way without changing
the stack, then make the second transition, the stack will not change altogether. This motivates the
addition of the rule Ap,q →aAr,sb for any such configuration.
Note that this is perfectly consistent with the logic we are trying to implement: Ar,s is supposed to
stand for strings that can lead from r to s without changing the stack. Thus, strings derived from
aAr,sb can lead from p to q without changing the stack, so Ap,q should be able to derive them by our
logic.

citations.snippet:
6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 9
Dor Minzer
So far we studied the models of DFAs, NFAs, PDAs and CFGs, and their power. By that, we mean the
classes of languages that they can recognize, i.e., regular languages and context free languages. While these
classes are important and they have some applications by themselves, the primary goal of this discussion was
to set up the correct mindset with respect to how to formalize computation. Today, we will define a much
more important and central computational model, known as Turing Machines (TMs in short). While on the
surface level TMs will look like a small variation on our models thus far, they are a completely different
beast, and in principle they are able to compute anything that a modern computer can.

Design a Turing machine for the language L = {w ∈{0, 1}∗| w = wR}.
Solution:
We start reading the input, look at its first symbol, remember it in our state and then replace

remember in our state. If it is not, we reject. If it is, we replace it by ⊥, go back to the first non ⊥symbol in
the input, and repeat the process. If we replaced the whole input with ⊥, we accept.

We now define the class of languages that can be recognized by Turing machines.
Definition 1.6. A language L ⊆Σ∗is called recursively enumerable if there exists a TM M such that
L(M) = L.

Solution:
1. Check that the input is of the form aibjck for some i, j, k ⩾1; else reject.
2. Return to the start of the tape. Delete one a and move to the b’s part. Zig-zagging between the b’s and
the c’s, remove one b and c at a time until all of the b’s run out. If the c’s run out before the b’s, reject.
3. Restore all of the b’s and go to step 2 if some a is still left.
4. If all of the a’s are deleted, check if all of the c’s are deleted, and if so accept. Else, reject.

k = ij. Note that step 2 reduces the number of c’s by j and the number of a’s is reduced by 1, so it reduces
the above check to the check that k −j = (i −1)j, which is equivalent to the check that k = ij. Finally,

Theorem 5. If M is a DFA with q states over ! = {0, 1}, then either |L(M)| ⇐2q, or else L(M)
is inﬁnite.
Proof. If M accepts some string of length at least q, then along the accepting computation we visit
q +1 states including the start state, so some state repeats by the pigeonhole principle. This means
there is a loop on the accepting path. Repeating that loop any number of times still allows the
machine to reach acceptance, so inﬁnitely many strings are accepted. Hence L(M) is inﬁnite.
So if L(M) is ﬁnite, then M accepts no string of length at least q. Therefore every accepted
string has length at most q ↔1.

b30001f8-8fe0-4d53-ac5e-422ccac59386.name: Language L↓ construction
b30001f8-8fe0-4d53-ac5e-422ccac59386.definition: A language consisting of strings that can be split into two parts where the left part ends with 0 and the right part has length r.

citations.snippet:
8.
8(a)
Theorem 7. L↓has an NFA with r + O(1) states.
Proof. The language Lr consists of strings ending in 0, and Sr consists of strings of length exactly
r. So L↓= Lr||Sr is the set of strings where there is some split point such that the left part ends
in 0 and the right part has length r.
An NFA can read the input and nondeterministically guess the split point. It stays in a scanning
state while reading an arbitrary preﬁx. Whenever it reads a 0, it may guess that this 0 is the last
symbol of the Lr part and then move into a chain of r states that reads exactly r more symbols.
It accepts if and only if the input ends exactly when the chain ﬁnishes.
This uses one scanning state plus a chain of r states and a constant number of additional states,
so the total is r + O(1) states.
